subject: comparing AKDE's with considerably different numbers of locations

messages.author: 1d6a3df3514fbc35
messages.subject: comparing AKDE's with considerably different numbers of locations
parts:
Good afternoon,

 

I have AKDE 95% and core homeranges based on birds with 4-6 locations a day, and I have homeranges from birds that have 30-120+ locations a day. Can I compare AKDE homeranges (95% and core) with that sort of GPS frequency disparity or would that be an inappropriate comparison to make due to the extreme difference in number of points each day?

 

Homeranges were calculated using methods in Buttler et al 2022, see below.

 

Butler, M.J., D.R. Stewart, G.M. Harris, M.T. Bidwell, and A.T. Pearse. 2022. Space use and site fidelity of wintering whooping cranes on the Texas Gulf Coast. Journal of Wildlife Management: e22226.

 

“We used the continuous‐time movement modeling (ctmm version 0.6.1) package for Program R version 4.0.5 (Fleming and Calabrese 2020, R CoreTeam 2021) to select and fit continuous‐time stochastic process models of movement and to estimate a home range using autocorrelated kernel density estimation (AKDE; Fleming et al. 2015, Calabrese et al. 2016, Fleming and Calabrese 2017). Traditional kernel density estimates (Worton 1989) do not allow for autocorrelated location data. Fleming et al. (2015) fully generalized the kernel density estimate to properly account for autocorrelation among locations in the ADKE. Once whooping cranes arrive on the wintering grounds, movements prior to settling into winter home ranges can be substantial and occur over several weeks. Therefore, we plotted locations, variograms, and outliers to determine an individual's movements and deleted GPS locations that were collected prior to a crane settling into its winter home range and outliers. Variograms plot the semi‐variance of locations as functions of the time lag between locations (Calabrese et al. 2016). Examination of the variogram reveals when individuals settle into a home range (i.e., variogram reaches an asymptote) and shows shifts in space use prior to settling into the home range (Calabrese et al. 2016). We indexed uncertainty in our location data with a categorical variable for fix quality (Pearse et al. 2020a). We used locations and fix quality from test transmitters (Pearse et al. 2017) and transmitters on carcasses to calibrate errors associated with our GPS devices (Fleming et al. 2016). This analysis related location error with fix quality and provided average error for each fix quality category. We assigned calibrated errors to the location data based on fix quality. Once we identified locations associated with range residency by an individual, we followed the workflow of Calabrese et al. (2016) to select and fit a movement model.

 

Traditional kernel density estimates of home range are underestimated when applied to serially autocorrelated data (Fleming et al. 2015). Therefore, we estimated home range areas using 95% AKDE based on the best fitting model. For comparison with previous work, we also estimated 95% and 50% minimum convex polygon (MCP) home ranges using the Program R package adehabitatHR version 0.4.19 (Calenge 2006).

 

For some individuals, location plots and abrupt changes on variograms suggested that some animals resided (were range resident) in multiple, distinct areas during a winter. In those situations, we fit different movement models to each period and estimated separate AKDEs and MCPs. If an individual had multiple home ranges within an overwintering period, we summed those home range areas for total winter home range area.

 

An animal's core home range is defined as the area of most concentrated use (Samuel et al. 1985, Seaman and Powell 1990). Often, the 50% isopleth of the kernel density is assumed as an appropriate core area, but differences in animal behavior or different distributions of resources within a home range can change intensity of space use across the home range (Vander Wal and Rodgers 2012). Therefore, we used an objective technique to determine the core isopleth of each home range instead of assuming 50% (Vander Wal and Rodgers 2012). To estimate the core isopleth and the core area of the AKDE home range for each individual, we determined the isopleth of the kernel density in which proportional use of the home range is equal to the predicted probability of use (Vander Wal and Rodgers 2012). Using nonlinear least‐squares (nls) regression in R, we regressed the proportional AKDE home range area as an exponential function of predicted probability of use (isopleth) for each home range. Isopleths used in this analysis were 10% to 90% in 10% increments, 95%, and 99%. The proportional area that each isopleth contained was based on the area of the 99% isopleth. We estimated the core area isopleth by setting the first derivative of the fitted nls model to one and solving for the isopleth value (Vander Wal and Rodgers 2012). If an individual had multiple home ranges within an overwintering period, we averaged core area isopleths for one estimate per bird per year.”

 

 

Thank you,

 

Carter G. Crouch, Ph.D.

Director of Gulf Coast Programs

messages.author: 40fd627580dd34f5
messages.subject: Re: comparing AKDE's with considerably different numbers of locations
parts:
Hi Carter,

Yes, absolutely. This is the advantage of basing everything on a selected continuous-time stochastic process. You may find that the selected model for the finer-scale data is different than that of the coarse-scale data. This is appropriate and what makes the distribution estimates comparable (because they don't have that sampling dependent bias from assuming the same autocorrelation structure or lack of autocorrelation).

Best,
Chris
